parameters.definition: Value of a one-in-a-million reduction in the risk of death for a US resident: the official value of a statistical life divided by one million, in November 2026 dollars. Population-average value, not adjusted for age.

value.basis: HHS standard values for 2026: VSL low $6.6M, central $14.1M, high $21.5M in 2025 dollars (https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2d83af5823915d81871334ee08ad03d9/Standard-RIA-Values-2026.pdf, read). Multiplied by 1.035 to reach November 2026 prices (my CPI assumption) and divided by 1e6. US DOT's figure ($13.7M in 2024 dollars, recalled; DOT pages returned 403) gives the same central value after the same adjustment.

parameters.definition: As micromortValueUsd.us, for a resident of Western Europe (EU-15, UK, Switzerland, Norway), in November 2026 US dollars at market exchange rates.

value.basis: Three routes. (a) OECD 2025 meta-analysis: base VSL USD 8.4M for the EU and 8.5M for the US in 2022 dollars, income elasticity 1 (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/mortality-risk-valuation-in-policy-assessment_76ca89a2-en/full-report/recommended-vsl-estimates-for-policy-analysis_9b41dca3.html; search snippet, page returned 403); about 9.4M in 2026 dollars. (b) Transfer from the US value at elasticity 1 with Western European GNI per capita about 0.55-0.6 of the US: 14.6 x 0.58 = 8.5. (c) Older European Commission and national practice (DG MOVE transport handbook about EUR 3.3M in 2016, UK about GBP 2.4M; both recalled) is about 4-5M today. Mid 7.0 is the geometric middle of 5 and 9.4; lo and hi span the routes.

parameters.definition: As micromortValueUsd.us, for a resident of the city of Buenos Aires, in November 2026 US dollars at the market exchange rate (the rate at which the household would actually pay for goods).

value.basis: Income-elasticity transfer: VSL_AR = VSL_US x (GNI per capita AR / US)^e. Atlas GNI per capita 2024: Argentina $13,530, US $83,490 (World Bank, https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GNP.PCAP.CD; search snippet), ratio 0.162. e = 1.0 (OECD 2025; Viscusi and Masterman 2017) gives 14.6 x 0.162 = 2.4; e = 1.5 (Robinson, Hammitt and O'Keeffe 2019 reference case, recalled) gives 14.6 x 0.065 = 0.95. City of Buenos Aires incomes are roughly 1.5 times the national average (my estimate), giving 3.6 at e = 1 and 2.7 at e = 1.2. A PPP income ratio (about 0.35) would give 5.1. Mid 3.0; lo and hi cover the elasticity, income premium and exchange-rate choices.

parameters.definition: Value of an hour of unpaid (leisure or chore) time for an adult, November 2026 dollars.

value.basis: HHS default for unpaid time: median pre-tax wage $24.43 less a 17% effective tax rate = $20.27 in 2025 dollars (https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2d83af5823915d81871334ee08ad03d9/Standard-RIA-Values-2026.pdf, read); x 1.035 = $21.0. US DOT values personal travel time at 50% of median household income per hour, which also comes to about $19-20 (recalled). Lo is 50% of the HHS figure (the fraction transport appraisal applies to a personal wage); hi is the after-tax mean wage of an above-median earner.

parameters.definition: As timeValueUsdPerHour.us, for Western Europe, November 2026 US dollars.

value.basis: HHS method applied to European wages. Median gross hourly earnings 2022: EU EUR 14.9, Germany 19.4, Netherlands 19.0 (Eurostat Structure of Earnings Survey, https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Earnings_statistics; search snippet); with France about 16.5, UK about 18, Italy 13, Spain 11 (recalled) the population-weighted Western European median is about EUR 16.4. Plus about 17% nominal growth to 2026 = 19.2; less about 29% income tax and employee contributions = 13.6; x 1.15 USD per EUR (assumed) = $15.7. Lo is half of that.

parameters.definition: As timeValueUsdPerHour.us, for the city of Buenos Aires, November 2026 US dollars at the official exchange rate.

value.basis: Average taxable wage of stable formal workers (RIPTE) ARS 1,915,879 a month in June 2026 (https://www.argentina.gob.ar/trabajo/seguridadsocial/ripte; search snippet), about ARS 2.15M by November; at ARS 1,555 per dollar (retail rate early November 2026, search snippet) = $1,380 a month = $8.1 an hour over 170 hours; less 17% employee contributions = $6.7. Informal workers (over a third of the workforce) earn roughly half, so the after-tax median across all workers is about $5-6. Lo is half the mid; hi is a professional's after-tax wage.

parameters.definition: Real annual rate at which a household trades money now for money later; used for the capital recovery factor.

value.basis: US regulatory analysis uses 3% and 7% real (OMB Circular A-4 of 2003, as applied in https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2d83af5823915d81871334ee08ad03d9/Standard-RIA-Values-2026.pdf, read). 3% is also the European Commission's social discount rate (recalled). Lo is the real after-tax return on safe savings; hi is the OMB upper rate, close to the real cost of consumer credit for a household that borrows.

parameters.definition: Annual cost of the marginal litre of storage space in an urban apartment (a closet shelf, under a bed), November 2026 dollars.

value.basis: Average US apartment rent $1,730 a month (Apartments.com, April 2026; search snippet) over about 900 sq ft (recalled) = $1.92 per sq ft a month = $248 per square metre a year; I use $232 (between that and the Apartment List median of $1,390). Usable stack 1.8 m at 50% fill = 900 litres per square metre, so average floor space costs 232 / 900 = $0.26 per litre-year. Marginal dead space is worth about a quarter of average floor space (my judgment; range 10-100%): 0.26 x 0.25 = $0.065. Market check: self-storage at about $1.2-1.5 per sq ft a month, stacked 2 m at 60% fill, is $0.13-0.16 per litre-year (recalled prices). European city rents per square metre are similar to US ones and Buenos Aires about 40% lower (two-room flat ARS 898,154 a month in September 2026, Zonaprop via search snippet, about $12 per square metre a month), but flats are smaller, so I keep one value.

parameters.definition: Annual cost of the marginal litre of storage space in a detached or terraced house (garage, basement, attic, spare closet), November 2026 dollars.

value.basis: US single-family rent about $1.2 per sq ft a month (about $2,200 for 1,800 sq ft; recalled) = $158 per square metre a year. Garage or unfinished basement space is valued at about 30% of living space: $47 per square metre a year, or 47 / 900 = $0.052 per litre-year on average. Houses usually have slack, so the marginal litre is worth about 40% of that: $0.02. Hi is living-space value at 60%; lo is a house with empty basement.

parameters.definition: Price of the model's preparedness goods in Western Europe relative to the United States (US = 1), tax included, at market exchange rates.

value.basis: No prices fetched. Judgment: branded outdoor and electronic goods cost 10-30% more than US pre-sales-tax prices because of 19-22% VAT (a Sawyer Mini is about EUR 30-35 against $29; recalled); FFP2 masks, bottled water and shelf-stable food are at or below US prices; US tariffs since 2025 have narrowed the gap on imported goods.

parameters.definition: Price of the model's preparedness goods in Buenos Aires relative to the United States (US = 1), at the official exchange rate, for goods as sold on Mercado Libre or in local shops.

value.basis: Samples at ARS 1,555 per dollar (search snippets; Mercado Libre product pages returned 403): generic battery CO alarm ARS 59,994 (6 x 9,999) = $39 against $25-35 in the US, ratio 1.1-1.5; portable CO detector ARS 89,900 = $58; Sawyer Mini filter ARS 209,033-242,576 = $134-156 through a cross-border reseller (Desertcart) against $29, ratio about 5, an upper bound for branded specialty imports with no local distributor. Staples (water, canned food, fuel, candles) are at or below US prices. Weighting generic locally stocked goods at 1.2-1.5, staples at 0.8-1.0 and branded imports at 2-5 gives about 1.4. Items differ by a factor of five, so an item-level override would be better than one index.

parameters.definition: Share of days on which the household is at home or close enough to reach its home supplies when an event begins. Quantiles are over my uncertainty about the population average, not over households.

value.basis: Nights away: about 2.3 billion US domestic person-trips a year at about 1.8 nights each (BTS average stay 1.6-2.1 nights, search snippet; trip count recalled) = 12 nights per person, plus about 2-3 nights abroad = about 15 nights, or 4% of the year. Household members usually travel together, and daytime absence at work still leaves supplies within reach, so presence is about 0.95. Lower for frequent travellers and for hazards that block the way home (earthquake during working hours).

parameters.definition: Share of urban US households with at least one car or light truck available.

value.basis: 92% of all US households have a vehicle (2023 ACS, via https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/11/14/1-in-10-americans-rarely-or-never-drive-a-car/, read). Urban adults are 2.6 times as likely as suburban ones to seldom or never drive (18% against 7%, same page), so I take 0.90 for urban households; lo is central cities only.

parameters.definition: Share of urban Western European households with at least one car.

value.basis: National shares are about 72-85% (Belgium 72.4%, Statbel via search snippet; Germany 77%, France 82%, UK 78%, recalled). Large cities are far lower (Brussels under 50% per the same snippet; Paris about 35%, Berlin and Amsterdam about 50%, London 56%, recalled) and mid-sized cities about 70%.

parameters.definition: Share of households in the city of Buenos Aires that own a car.

value.basis: 38.3% of city households owned a car in the 2012 Encuesta Anual de Hogares (Direccion General de Estadistica y Censos, https://www.estadisticaciudad.gob.ar; search snippet); no newer figure found. I assume little change since.

parameters.definition: Share of US households whose main cooktop is electric, so that cooking stops when the grid fails. Gas cooktops can be lit with a match; gas ovens usually cannot.

value.basis: About 38% of US households cook with natural gas (EIA RECS 2020, https://www.eia.gov/pressroom/releases/press510.php; search snippet, page returned 503) and about 4% with propane (recalled), some of them alongside an electric appliance, leaving about 60% with an electric cooktop only.

parameters.definition: Share of Western European households whose main hob is electric (resistance, ceramic or induction).

value.basis: France 59% electric hobs (CLASP survey, https://www.clasp.ngo/research/all/consumer-survey-gas-electric-cooking/; search snippet); Italy 68-80% gas (same source). With Germany about 92%, Spain 70%, UK 42%, Netherlands 45% and the Nordic and Alpine countries about 90% electric (recalled), the population-weighted share is 0.62.

parameters.definition: Share of households in the city of Buenos Aires that cook mainly with electricity.

value.basis: 2022 census, city of Buenos Aires: electricity 14.8% (1.3% in 2010), mains gas 78.5% (https://estadisticaciudad.gob.ar/eyc/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ir_2024_1877.pdf; search snippet). New buildings are all-electric, so I add about two points for 2026.

parameters.definition: Share of US households whose main heating system stops when the grid fails (electric heating, heat pumps, and gas, oil or propane furnaces and boilers that need electric blowers, pumps, igniters or controls). Not net of secondary sources such as fireplaces.

value.basis: Recalled from EIA RECS 2020: main heating fuel is electricity for about 41% of households and gas, propane or oil through central equipment for most of the rest; grid-independent main heating is limited to wood stoves (about 2%) and unpowered gas wall, floor or room heaters with standing pilots (about 3-5%, mostly older homes in the South and California). In Texas in 2021, 26% of those who stayed home heated with a gas oven or cooktop (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf), which shows how few had a working alternative. Perhaps 20% of households, nearly all in houses, also have a fireplace or stove that works unpowered.

parameters.definition: As shareHeatingNeedsGrid.us, for Western Europe.

value.basis: Judgment. Gas and oil boilers with pumped radiators, district heating substations, heat pumps and direct electric heating all stop. Exceptions: log stoves as main heating (a few percent; a further fifth of households in France and Germany have one as a secondary source, mostly in houses) and bottled-gas room heaters in Spain and Portugal.

parameters.definition: As shareHeatingNeedsGrid.us, for the city of Buenos Aires.

value.basis: Judgment, no source found. Balanced-flue gas room heaters, which need no electricity, are the traditional main heating; the rest use reverse-cycle air conditioners, portable electric heaters or building central systems with electric pumps. Winters are mild (July mean minimum about 7-8 C), so cold exposure is modest in any case.

parameters.definition: Among apartment households, the share whose taps run dry within about a day of a building power failure even though the street main stays pressurised (buildings that rely on electric booster pumps or pumped roof tanks).

value.basis: Mains pressure serves roughly the first five or six floors; taller buildings need booster pumps. About a tenth of US apartment units are in buildings of seven or more storeys (recalled from the American Housing Survey), plus some mid-rise buildings in low-pressure zones. New York roof tanks held for less than a day in the 2003 blackout. Failure of the utility's own pumping is the hazard files' business, not this parameter.

parameters.definition: As shareApartmentPumpedWater.us, for Western Europe.

value.basis: Mostly three- to six-storey blocks on mains pressure in Germany, France, the Netherlands and the UK, but communal booster pumps are common in Spain and Italy: in the April 2025 blackout Spanish buildings with pressure groups lost water above about the second or third floor (https://www.xatakahome.com/hogar/que-agua-salga-poca-fuerza-problemon-hay-muchas-soluciones-solo-legal-funciona-no-deja-secos-a-vecinos and the Malaga water company notice, search snippets).

parameters.definition: As shareApartmentPumpedWater.us, for the city of Buenos Aires.

value.basis: Judgment from how buildings are plumbed, no source found: apartment buildings take water into a ground-level cistern and pump it to a roof tank that feeds the flats by gravity, so when the pump stops the building has only the roof tank, typically half a day to a day of normal use. Only ground-floor units and low buildings on direct mains connection are spared.

parameters.definition: Share of US households with air conditioning (central or room units).

value.basis: 88% of 123.5 million households (EIA RECS 2020, search snippet) and more than 90% (US Census Bureau, cited in https://www.carbonbrief.org/eight-facts-about-air-conditioning-amid-an-overheated-global-debate/, read). Much lower in a few places (Seattle, San Francisco: about half, recalled).

parameters.definition: Share of Western European households with air conditioning.

value.basis: Europe about 20% (IEA); Italy nearly 60%, Spain 41%, France 25%, Germany 6% (Verivox says 19% in 2024), UK under 5% (all from https://www.carbonbrief.org/eight-facts-about-air-conditioning-amid-an-overheated-global-debate/, read). Population-weighted with 20% for the Netherlands and 12% elsewhere: 0.22 with Germany at 6%, 0.25 with Germany at 19%.

parameters.definition: Share of households in the city of Buenos Aires with air conditioning.

value.basis: 47.1% of households nationally (INDEC household energy survey 2017-18, via La Nacion, search snippet). The city is richer and hotter in summer than the national average and ownership has grown since, so I add about 20 points.

parameters.definition: Money cost per person per day of staying away from home beyond normal living costs (lodging and the extra cost of meals), averaged over the ways people relocate. Excludes the hardship of displacement itself.

value.basis: Hotel route: GSA standard lodging rate for fiscal 2027 is $113 a night (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/10/2026-18439/maximum-per-diem-reimbursement-rates-for-the-continental-united-states-conus; search snippet), shared by 2.5 people = $45 each, plus meals out at part of the $68 meals rate less about $12 of groceries saved = about $35: $80 per person-day for a family, about $150 for one person alone; I use $95 for this route. Friends-or-family route: about $15 for contributions and extra travel. Evacuation surveys put roughly 60% with friends or relatives, 30% in paid lodging and the rest in shelters (recalled): 0.6 x 15 + 0.3 x 95 + 0.1 x 10 = $38; I round up to 45 because multi-day events fill cheap rooms.

parameters.definition: As relocationUsdPerPersonDay.us, for Western Europe, US dollars.

value.basis: No separate data found. Hotel rates and restaurant prices are close to US levels and the split between relatives and paid lodging is assumed the same.

parameters.definition: As relocationUsdPerPersonDay.us, for Buenos Aires, US dollars.

value.basis: Judgment: mid-range hotels about $60-90 a night and meals out about $15-25 a day (recalled), and a larger share staying with family: 0.7 x 8 + 0.3 x 45 = $19.

parameters.definition: One-off cost per household of leaving and returning: transport both ways and the adults' travel and packing time.

value.basis: 300-mile round trip at $0.30 a mile marginal cost = $90; two adults x 5 hours of travel and packing x $21 = $210; total $300. Lo is a short drive to relatives counted at fuel cost only; hi is flights or a congested mass evacuation.

parameters.definition: As relocationFixedUsdPerHousehold.us, for Western Europe, US dollars.

value.basis: Shorter distances and a third of urban households without a car: train or car for 200 km each way, about $100, plus two adults x 4 hours x $15 = $120.

parameters.definition: As relocationFixedUsdPerHousehold.us, for Buenos Aires, US dollars.

value.basis: Bus or car to a city 300-400 km away: about $55 in fares or fuel plus two adults x 5 hours x $5.5 = $55.

parameters.definition: Days from the start of a major rich-country disaster until organised relief (water, food, shelter supplies) reaches the median affected household that needs it. The value is my uncertainty about that median. Across households and events I put the 10th percentile at 1 day, the median at 3, the 90th percentile at 7 and the 99th at 21 days.

value.basis: Cases: Sandy 2012, city distribution points opened 3 days after landfall (recalled); Katrina 2005, relief and buses reached the Superdome on days 3-5 (prior-art.md); Texas 2021, mass water distribution from about day 4-5 while 63% reported difficulty finding bottled water (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf); Helene 2024, officials still promising water and food on day 3, helicopter drops that day, Red Cross distribution centres running about day 10 (https://fortune.com/2024/10/01/supplies-north-carolina-plane-truck-mule-hurricane-helene-death-toll-130/ and Red Cross reports, search snippets); Andrew 1992, on day 8 a quarter of households depended on relief food, so relief was reaching them by then (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00017631.htm); Maria 2017, weeks for interior municipalities. The official '72 hours' rests on an assumption, not on measurement (prior-art.md). No systematic dataset exists.

parameters.definition: Willingness to pay of a household with no backup to avoid one day without grid electricity, excluding risk of death, November 2026 dollars. Scaling with duration: the first 8 hours carry about 55% of the first day's cost ($29.42 of $53.68); from day 1 to about day 10 the cost per day is roughly constant; beyond two weeks there is no evidence. Does not include the one-off loss of refrigerated food.

value.basis: LBNL ICE 2.0: residential willingness to pay $1.90 momentary, $7.08 for 2 h, $29.42 for 8 h, $53.68 for 24 h (90% CI 49.98-57.38), rural cooperative members (https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ice_2.0_nreca_final_report_28oct2026.pdf, read). Baik et al. 2020: $43-60 a day in 2018 dollars for partial backup through a 10-day winter blackout (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-0581-1, verified in prior-art.md), about $56-78 today. FEMA residential value $33.04 per person-day in 2022 dollars x 2.5 people x 1.14 = $94 (https://fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_standard-economic-values-methodology-report_2023.pdf, verified in prior-art.md). Mid 65 sits between ICE and FEMA; hi allows for willingness to accept exceeding willingness to pay by two to three times.

parameters.definition: Welfare loss per person per day without any tap water, for all household uses (drinking, cooking, washing, flushing), excluding risk of death, November 2026 dollars. Scaling with duration: FEMA applies the same value to every day; I would halve it on day 1 (liquids and cistern water on hand) and hold it flat after that. Stored drinking water at 4 litres a day replaces only part of this loss, perhaps a third to a half.

value.basis: FEMA standard value for residential loss of potable water: $74.38 per person-day in 2022 dollars (welfare loss $66.26 plus $8.12 for bottled water at 6.6 gallons), or $138 including economic activity (https://fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_standard-economic-values-methodology-report_2023.pdf, verified in prior-art.md). x 1.14 for inflation to November 2026 (my CPI assumption) = $85 and $157. Lo is half the residential value.

parameters.definition: Risk of death in a disaster for a child under 15 relative to an adult aged 15-59, all causes combined. Infants are well above this average and older children below it.

value.basis: Rate ratios from deaths by age (read from the sources) over population by age (recalled census shares, so each ratio is good to about 20%). Texas 2021: ages 0-19, 8 deaths in 8.25M against 90 in 15.5M aged 20-59: 0.17 (https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/news/updates/SMOC_FebWinterStorm_MortalitySurvReport_12-30-21.pdf; population shares approximate). Katrina: under 18, 1 per 10,000 against about 6.6 for ages 18-59: 0.15 (https://doi.org/10.1097/DMP.0b013e31818aaf55, Table 2). British Columbia 2021: no deaths under 19 (https://nanaimo.ca/docs/public-safety-department/bc-coroners-reportheat_related_deaths_in_bc_knowledge_update.cleaned.pdf). Japan 2011 indirect deaths: 1 of 1,263 under 10: 0.08 (https://www.reconstruction.go.jp/topics/20120821_shinsaikanrenshihoukoku.pdf). Ordinary all-cause mortality gives about 0.2.

parameters.definition: Risk of death in a disaster for a person aged 60-74 relative to an adult aged 15-59, all causes combined. Cold and injury sit at the low end, heat and interrupted care at the high end.

value.basis: Texas 2021: ages 60-79, 100 deaths in 4.55M = 22.0 per million against 5.8 for ages 20-59: 3.8 (https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/news/updates/SMOC_FebWinterStorm_MortalitySurvReport_12-30-21.pdf). Katrina: about 32 per 10,000 at 55-74 against 6.6: 4.8 (https://doi.org/10.1097/DMP.0b013e31818aaf55). British Columbia heat: 164 per million at 60-69 and 338 at 70-79 against 15.3 at 15-59, about 12 for 60-74 (https://nanaimo.ca/docs/public-safety-department/bc-coroners-reportheat_related_deaths_in_bc_knowledge_update.cleaned.pdf). Japan indirect deaths: about 10 (https://www.reconstruction.go.jp/topics/20120821_shinsaikanrenshihoukoku.pdf; population shares approximate). New York 2003: 65-74 against under 65, 48 against 3.8 per million: 12.6 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3276729). Ordinary all-cause mortality: about 6.

parameters.definition: Risk of death in a disaster for a person aged 75 or over relative to an adult aged 15-59, all causes combined. About 10 for cold and injury, 45 or more for heat and for the indirect deaths of evacuation and interrupted care.

value.basis: Texas 2021: ages 80+, 47 deaths in 0.85M = 55 per million against 5.8: 9.5 (https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/news/updates/SMOC_FebWinterStorm_MortalitySurvReport_12-30-21.pdf). Katrina: 121 per 10,000 against 6.6: 18 (https://doi.org/10.1097/DMP.0b013e31818aaf55). New York 2003: 75+ against under 65: 87 against 3.8 per million = 23 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3276729). British Columbia heat: 747 per million at 80-89 and 1,388 at 90+ against 15.3: about 45 for 75+ (https://nanaimo.ca/docs/public-safety-department/bc-coroners-reportheat_related_deaths_in_bc_knowledge_update.cleaned.pdf). Japan indirect deaths: 80+ are 68% of deaths and about 8% of population: about 73 for 75+ (https://www.reconstruction.go.jp/topics/20120821_shinsaikanrenshihoukoku.pdf). Ordinary all-cause mortality: about 30.

deaths.basis: Lo is the 246 deaths certified by the state (https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/news/updates/SMOC_FebWinterStorm_MortalitySurvReport_12-30-21.pdf, read). Mid and hi are the BuzzFeed News excess-death estimate for the week ending 20 February, 702 (426-978) (https://www.kut.org/energy-environment/2021-05-27/texas-winter-storm-death-toll-could-be-much-higher-than-the-states-estimate-buzzfeed-review-found, read); the uncounted deaths were mostly medically vulnerable people with cardiovascular disease, diabetes or kidney problems.

exposedPersons.basis: People in homes that lost power: 69% of respondents (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf; survey of the ERCOT area, about 90% of the state's 29.1 million) = 18-20 million; mid 19 million.

exposureDays.basis: Mean time without power 42 hours, median 36 (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf); hi allows for homes that stayed cold after power returned.

micromortsPerExposedPersonDay.basis: mid = 700 / (19,000,000 x 1.75) x 1e6; lo = lowest deaths over highest exposure, hi = highest deaths over lowest exposure, so the range is wider than a 90% interval.

anchors.notes: Per Texas resident (29.1 million) rather than per person without power: 8.5 micromorts on the certified count, 24 on the excess estimate, over the whole event. The certified count gives 7.4 per person-day without power.

deaths.basis: Lo is certified extreme-cold deaths: 158 hypothermia and 3 frostbite (https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/news/updates/SMOC_FebWinterStorm_MortalitySurvReport_12-30-21.pdf). Hi applies the certified cold share (65.4%) to the upper excess estimate (978). Mid is halfway between 161 and 65.4% of the central excess estimate (459), on the view that part of the uncounted excess was cold-triggered cardiovascular death.

exposedPersons.basis: People in homes that lost power: 69% of respondents (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf; survey of the ERCOT area, about 90% of the state's 29.1 million) = 18-20 million; mid 19 million.

exposureDays.basis: Mean time without power 42 hours, median 36 (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf); hi allows for homes that stayed cold after power returned.

micromortsPerExposedPersonDay.basis: mid = 300 / (19,000,000 x 1.75) x 1e6; lo = lowest deaths over highest exposure, hi = highest deaths over lowest exposure, so the range is wider than a 90% interval.

anchors.notes: Certified count alone gives 4.8. Of the 158 hypothermia deaths 107 (67.7%) were aged 60 or over and 13.9% involved alcohol. Some died outdoors or homeless, so not every death belongs to a home without power. Overnight lows were about -7 C in Houston and -15 C or below in north Texas (recalled).

deaths.basis: 158 hypothermia deaths less 107 aged 60 or over = 51 (https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/news/updates/SMOC_FebWinterStorm_MortalitySurvReport_12-30-21.pdf); lo drops a share for deaths outdoors unrelated to home power, hi scales by the excess-to-certified ratio.

exposedPersons.basis: People under 60 in homes that lost power: 82% of 19 million (Texas age structure, approximate).

exposureDays.basis: Mean time without power 42 hours, median 36 (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf); hi allows for homes that stayed cold after power returned.

openQuestions: Most deaths the model can avert are of people aged 75 or over, with perhaps eight discounted life-years left. A population-average micromort value overstates them about threefold relative to a life-year approach (HHS value per statistical life year $611,000 at 3%). Official US practice does not adjust for age and the OECD advises against it, so I give the unadjusted value, but the engine should offer a per-life-year option.

To compare an all-ages anchor with a healthy-adult mortality curve, divide the anchor by the population-average multiplier. With US age shares (under 15, 18%; 15-59, 59%; 60-74, 16%; 75 and over, 7%) and the multipliers here it is 0.18 x 0.15 + 0.59 + 0.16 x 7 + 0.07 x 25 = 3.5. Texas cold: 9.0 / 3.5 = 2.6 micromorts per healthy-adult day without power, which agrees with the direct under-60 figure of 1.9-2.9.

Age multipliers differ by cause by a factor of five (about 10 at 75 and over for cold and injury, 45-75 for heat and interrupted care). Need-level multipliers from the item researchers should override these cross-cutting ones where they exist.

Anchor denominators mix two conventions: people in homes that lost a utility (Texas, Irma, Sandy) and all residents (New York, British Columbia, Japan, Maria, Iberia). The notes give the alternative where it changes the figure by more than a factor of 1.5.

Excess-death estimates are two to four times the certified counts (Texas 702 against 246; Irma; Iberia 147 against 8). Mortality curves fitted to certified counts will understate harm to the old and chronically ill by about that factor.
priceIndex for Buenos Aires hides a fivefold spread between locally stocked goods and branded imports; item-level availability and price would be better.
storageCostUsdPerLitreYear is given by dwelling type only. Rents per square metre differ by location (Buenos Aires about 40% below US levels), but so do dwelling sizes; I did not split it.
The November 2026 price level is my assumption (3.5% above the 2025 average, 14% above 2022); replace with the published CPI.
homePresence is an annual average. Absence is correlated with some hazards (holiday travel in winter storms, summer holidays in heat waves) and warning brings people home before others.

shareHeatingNeedsGrid counts main heating only. The share of households with a secondary heat source that works unpowered (fireplace, wood stove, unpowered gas heater) is the warmth researcher's baseline and I have only a rough 20% for US houses.
